content: Nutmeg liver, also known as cardiac cirrhosis, refers to the pathological appearance of the liver caused by chronic passive congestion secondary to right heart failure. The liver exhibits a speckled appearance, resembling a grated nutmeg kernel. This is due to the presence of dilated, congested central veins (dark spots) interspersed with paler, unaffected surrounding liver tissue. In severe and prolonged cases, hepatic congestion can progress to cirrhosis, a condition termed cardiac cirrhosis. Pathophysiology The condition arises from increased pressure in the sublobular branches of the hepatic veins, leading to venous blood engorgement. This is most commonly associated with chronic cardiac lesions, particularly those affecting the right side of the heart. The impaired cardiac function causes blood to back up into the inferior vena cava and hepatic veins, resulting in passive congestion of the liver. Gross Pathology The central regions of the hepatic lobules appear red or brown, contrasting with the tan-colored, non-congested liver tissue. Centrilobular necrosis is a hallmark feature. Macroscopically, the liver exhibits a pale and spotty appearance in affected areas. This is due to blood stasis, which causes pericentral hepatocytes (liver cells near the central veins) to become deoxygenated compared to the relatively better-oxygenated periportal hepatocytes (liver cells near the hepatic arterioles). This pattern of blood flow impairment is also observed in pulmonary lesions, such as chronic interstitial pneumonia, pleural effusions, and intrathoracic tumors. Pathological Findings Images of nutmeg liver demonstrate the characteristic gross appearance, with a natural color pattern resembling a nutmeg kernel. The congested central hepatic veins appear as pale spots, and the liver's cut surface closely mimics the texture and coloration of a polished nutmeg. These findings are often associated with chronic passive congestion and liver fibrosis due to congestive heart failure. Symptoms The clinical presentation of nutmeg liver depends largely on the underlying cardiac or pulmonary conditions causing it. Patients may experience a sense of fullness and tenderness in the right hypochondriac region. Gastrointestinal symptoms, such as catarrh, are common, and hematemesis may occur. Jaundice is frequently observed to varying degrees. Portal vein obstruction can lead to ascites, which may progress to generalized edema (dropsy). Stools are often light or clay-colored, while urine may be darkened due to bile pigments. On physical examination, the liver is typically enlarged and tender, sometimes extending several inches below the costal margin of the ribs. Treatment Management of nutmeg liver primarily focuses on addressing the underlying cause. If the root cause cannot be eliminated, efforts are directed toward mitigating its effects. This includes implementing hygienic and dietary measures, even in cases where the condition is due to valvular heart lesions.
